title: Rahul Agarwal's Fold-Flat Spoon Wins $350,000 Shark Tank Deal
excerpt: Polygons founder Rahul Agarwal took $350,000 from Lori Greiner and Mindy Kaling for 8% equity plus 2% advisory shares, valuing the fold-flat measuring spoon business below his $5 million ask.
body:
• Rahul Agarwal, the Jersey City-based founder of Polygons Design Inc., secured a $350,000 deal on Shark Tank Season 18 for his fold-flat measuring spoons — $350,000 for 8% equity plus 2% in advisory shares from Lori Greiner and guest Shark Mindy Kaling.
  • Polygons replaces a six-piece measuring spoon set with two 2.8 mm flat tools that fold into six measures; the company says it has sold more than 200,000 units in over 110 countries and won more than 20 international design awards.
  • Agarwal asked for $350,000 for 7% at a $5 million valuation, citing about $4 million in lifetime sales; Kevin O'Leary also offered $350,000, first for 15% and then 10%, before Agarwal chose the Greiner-Kaling joint deal.
  • For diaspora shoppers: the two-spoon set sells for $29.99 at getpolygons.com and on Amazon — buy only from those two stores, the company warns, after more than 4,600 counterfeit listings were taken down.

Rahul Agarwal walked into the Shark Tank seeking $350,000 for 7% of Polygons, his fold-flat measuring spoon company, and walked out with a joint deal from Lori Greiner and guest Shark Mindy Kaling. The final on-screen agreement, in the Season 18 episode aired October 14, was $350,000 for 8% equity plus 2% in advisory shares, according to Shark Tank Insights' episode breakdown. Kaling called the product ingenious in the show's own clip of the pitch.

A spoon redesigned from a dare

Agarwal was a student at India's National Institute of Design in 2014 when a senior told him not to bother redesigning objects that had already reached their final form — for example, a spoon. He took it as a dare. "I don't even cook," he said in the company's Globe Newswire announcement of the appearance. "I just couldn't leave it alone." Within three days he had the core idea: a flat sheet that folds into an exact measure when pinched at a marked point.

The finished set uses two tools, each 2.8 mm thin. The large spoon gives 1/2, 1 and 2 tablespoons; the small one gives 1/4, 1/2 and 1 teaspoon. Flattened again, it scrapes honey or peanut butter from a jar and wipes clean in one pass, and hidden magnets keep both spoons on the fridge. Turning that idea into a durable product took almost three years, more than 1,000 prototypes and seven manufacturers, the company says.

"We entered a 3,000-year-old category and walked out with 20+ international design awards."

— Rahul Agarwal, Founder, Polygons Design Inc.

The numbers the Sharks tested

The Sharks pressed Agarwal on sales, costs and customer acquisition. He put lifetime sales at about $4 million, with $1.25 million in the last year on one account of the pitch, a manufacturing cost of $7 against a $24 to $29 selling price, and a customer acquisition cost of $7.50 across Amazon, TikTok Shop and the company's own website. Kendra Scott noted that Agarwal drew only $500 a month for himself from the business. Robert Herjavec went out, concerned that shoppers would need educating to pay $24 for a function a $2 spoon set performs; Scott also passed, saying the product did not fit her niche.

The company's longer record helped carry the pitch. Polygons began as a 2016 Kickstarter campaign that raised $1,022,120 from 36,863 backers against a $10,000 goal, though backers waited years for delivery as manufacturing slipped. It has since sold more than 200,000 units in over 110 countries, holds U.S. Patent No. 10,175,084, was selected by the MoMA Design Store, and counts two Red Dot Awards and an iF DESIGN AWARD among its honours, according to the company announcement and All Shark Tank Products' history of the business. You can watch the pitch segment via Shark Tank Global on YouTube.

What happens next

Televised Shark Tank deals are not final until due diligence closes, and no closing has been publicly confirmed for Polygons. What is confirmed is distribution: the set is on sale now for $29.99 in eight colours at getpolygons.com and the official Polygons store on Amazon. For an Indian design-school idea that began in Ahmedabad and is now designed in India, made in China and sold from Jersey City, the Greiner-Kaling backing — retail reach from Greiner, cultural reach from Kaling — is the next test of whether a premium spoon can become a standard American kitchen drawer item.
